Tuan Sing to open Opus Bay integrated resort in Batam this December
article:
Singapore-listed developer Tuan Sing Holdings Limited will begin the phased opening of Opus Bay, the first integrated resort in Batam, Indonesia, from December.

The first phase includes Marina Bay Ferry Cove, the resort’s own ferry terminal, and Residence on Opus Bay. The latter comprises two properties: the 493-key Balmoral Tower hotel and Cluny Resorts, an ultra-luxury villa retreat scheduled to open in 2027.

Balmoral Tower will be Batam’s largest hotel, spanning 35 storeys. It offers nine room types, from studios to two-bedroom suites. All rooms will come with private balconies, kitchenettes, washer-dryers and an AI-powered digital concierge.

Meanwhile, Cluny Resorts will feature 57 villas across seven categories, ranging from 1,819 sq ft one-bedders to a three-bedroom Grand Villa measuring 5,899 sq ft.

Opus Bay is located within a 45-minute ferry ride from Singapore. The integrated resort will also have a waterfront retail and dining precinct, Bay Boulevard Marina Promenade, with around 80 stores. Spanning 107,640 sq ft, the retail promenade will include a food hall and supermarket.

Guests will be able to enjoy tourist attractions and amenities at Saung Budaya Batam, a living cultural house and traditional arts space; Puncak Beliung, a scenic hilltop eco -tourism destination; and Batam Hills Golf Resort. They are about a 10-minute drive from Opus Bay.

Retail options at Grand Batam Mall, Batam City Square and K-Square are also a 30- to 35-minute drive away.

title: What Japan's rising land prices really tell us about the property market
article:
Japan's latest land price data confirms something those of us in the property market have been seeing for some time now. Land prices are rising again, and the recovery is getting broader.

The latest government survey showed nationwide land prices increasing for a fifth consecutive year, with residential and commercial land both appreciating, and particularly strong gains in the major metropolitan areas.

For a country where falling property values shaped investment decisions for decades, that's a meaningful shift.

But the national number hides more than it reveals.

Japan is not one property market. It comprises dozens of them. What moves a residential building in central Tokyo has almost nothing to do with what moves a hotel in Nagoya or a house in a regional city.

Higher costs and the appeal of older condos

In Tokyo, one of the clearest pressures is simply the cost and scarcity of creating new supply in desirable locations.

Well-located land is limited and construction materials, labor and development costs have all risen sharply.

That combination makes it more expensive to build something new, and it raises the value of existing buildings that are structurally sound and well located.

It is part of why we have spent so many years acquiring older condos and renovating them rather than starting from scratch.

New-build condos in central Tokyo tend to be small — developers size units down to hit affordable price points, given how expensive land and construction have become.

That leaves a gap for buyers who want more space than a new building can offer at a comparable price.

Older condos, many of them originally built with more generous floor plans, fill that gap naturally.

Renovated to reflect what today's buyers actually want — more bathrooms and toilets, for instance — they can be just as compelling as new construction, often at a better price for the space.

How tourism and the weak yen are influencing demand

International visitors have added another layer of demand. According to the Japan National Tourism Organization , Japan welcomed a record 42.68 million international visitors in 2025, up 15.8% from the year before.

That momentum carried into 2026 — July alone brought 3.44 million arrivals , the highest figure ever recorded for that month.

The effect can be seen most clearly in Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto, where hotels, restaurants and retail now compete directly with residential and commercial users for the same square footage.

In some tourism-heavy markets, the impact on land values has been striking; the latest survey showed particularly strong appreciation in destinations that benefit most from inbound demand.

There is also a less obvious link between tourism and investment. Most international buyers' first exposure to Japanese real estate is simply spending time here — the trains, the safety, the quality of construction, the restaurants and the neighborhoods.

Only later does that familiarity turn into an interest in owning something: a residence, an investment property, or a broader allocation to Japan.

The weak yen has made that conversation an easier one to have. Convert a Tokyo property’s value into Singapore dollars or US dollars and it can look inexpensive next to other major global cities.

But currency is only one part of the case, and it is the part most likely to change. Exchange rates move constantly. A building's location, tenant base and physical condition do not.

That is why, when we look at a property, we spend far more time on the neighborhood and the building than on any macro narrative.

Who wants to live there? How good is the transportation? Is rental demand durable, and how much competing supply could realistically get built nearby? Can the property itself be improved?

Those questions, not the macro numbers, are what decide whether an asset holds up over time.

Closer look at Japan's major property markets

National averages can also be misleading in the other direction — they understate what is happening in the strongest markets.

The 2026 government land survey found that prices in the Tokyo and Osaka metropolitan areas rose considerably faster than the national average.

Tokyo has the underlying fundamentals on its side: a steady inflow of population, a vast employment base, deep housing demand and transportation infrastructure most cities can only aim for.

Osaka is building its own momentum, with substantial investment flowing in.

Kyoto has a different character altogether — global tourism demand running into supply that is unusually constrained by geography and history.

Beyond these three, conditions vary enormously by region.

We have made a bet on that kind of local distinction ourselves. LogProstyle built its business primarily in Greater Tokyo, but this September we completed the acquisition of I-Flatz , a condo sales, renovation and leasing company focusing on Osaka and Kyoto in the Kansai region.

The deal gives us a platform to bring the business model we have proven over the past 20 years in Greater Tokyo to Kansai, Japan's second-largest economic region after Kanto — adapted to how business actually works there, not just copied from Tokyo.

Consumer preferences are different there. So is the available housing stock, tourism patterns, and what you can and cannot build. Real estate investment that ignores those differences does not tend to work out.

What comes next for property investors

Rates are moving too. Japan is stepping away from the extraordinarily loose monetary policy that defined the past few decades.

The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, the highest it's been in 31 years.

Borrowing costs now matter more in every acquisition decision we make.

Still, it is worth keeping in perspective that mortgage rates for buyers remain very low by global standards, even after this normalisation, and our own average cost of debt at LogProstyle is still under 3% — low next to what borrowers face in most other developed markets.

If you are an international investor — and I hear this most often from people looking at Japan out of Singapore — the useful move is to get specific, fast.

A national land-price index tells you which way the wind is blowing. It will not tell you whether a given building, on a given street, with a given tenant base, is actually a good investment.

That is a different question, and it has to be answered property by property.

Five straight years of nationwide increases tell us the recovery has real breadth, not just a few hot spots carrying the average.

What comes next is harder: investors will have to tell markets apart from each other, city by city, and sometimes street by street.

Japan's major cities still have limited supply, international demand and a lot of ageing buildings worth a second look.

Those forces are real. But the opportunities that last will keep coming from the same place they always have — understanding why people actually want to live, visit and invest somewhere.

Yasuyuki Nozawa is representative director, president and CEO of LogProstyle , a Tokyo-headquartered, New York-listed real estate platform spanning condo renovation and resale, residential development, investor-oriented property operations, ryokan hotel operations and restaurant brands.

title: Get Smart: One Lot of DBS For S$14,000?
article:
When I first started buying Singapore stocks in 2012, one thing shocked me.
You needed a lot of money just to get started.
Back then, a standard SGX board lot was 1,000 shares.
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05) traded at an average of about S$13.98 in 2012. That meant buying just one lot could cost nearly S$14,000.
And
Jardine Cycle & Carriage Ltd (SGX: C07)
? Its shares traded above S$40 during 2012. At those prices, a single 1,000-share lot would have required more than S$40,000.
I remember looking at stocks like DBS,
Singapore Exchange Ltd
(SGX: S68), and Jardine Cycle & Carriage and thinking: gosh, that is a lot of money just to buy one company.
What was worse was that it was not always the amount I actually wanted to invest.
Sometimes, it was simply the minimum I was allowed to buy.
More than a decade ago, David Kuo was already making the same point.
In 2014, he argued that Singapore’s 1,000-share board lots were unnecessarily restrictive and that smaller lots would make higher-priced shares more accessible to ordinary investors.
A year later, SGX reduced the standard board lot from 1,000 shares to 100.
Now, more than a decade on, we have taken another step.
When the board lot decides your portfolio for you
Imagine you had S$20,000 to invest back then.
You liked
DBS
. You did your homework.
But if one lot cost close to S$14,000, buying it would have put roughly 70% of your portfolio into a single company.
Not because you wanted 70% in DBS.
Simply because that was how shares were packaged.
Ideally, investing should start with:
How much of my portfolio do I want to put into this company?
But under the old system, the question could easily become:
Can I afford one lot?
Those are very different questions.
From 1,000 shares to 100, and now 10
From 5 October 2026, SGX
cut board lots
further for higher-priced securities.
For stocks priced above S$10 and up to $100, the board lot can now be 10 shares. Securities above S$100 can trade in single-share lots.
The first batch covered 11 counters, including DBS,
United Overseas Bank Ltd
(SGX: U11),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), SGX and
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) .
And investors have already embraced the change.
The Business Times reported that on the first day of the revised framework, DBS recorded about 5,000 trades in 10-share lots.
Across the 11 counters, more than 20,000 trades were executed in 10-share lots, compared with more than 13,000 in 100-share lots.
In fact, 55% of all trades across the 11 counters were below the previous 100-share board lot.
A good company can still be too big a position
We spend a lot of time asking whether a stock is good.
Is the company growing? Is its balance sheet strong? Can it grow dividends? Is the valuation reasonable?
But another question matters too:
Even if I like this stock, how much should I own?
Take a stock trading at S$50.
With a 100-share board lot, the minimum investment is S$5,000.
With a 10-share board lot, it is S$500.
The business has not changed.
What has changed is your ability to control the size of your investment.
That matters, especially if you are starting with $10,000 or $20,000.
A minimum purchase of several thousand dollars can dominate a portfolio very quickly.
Smaller lots make it easier to spread your money across several companies, keep cash aside, or simply take a smaller initial position.
You do not have to make one big decision
There is another benefit.
Investing often feels binary: buy or do not buy.
But it does not have to work that way.
You might like a company but think the
valuation
is only fair.
Instead of committing several thousand dollars immediately, you can start smaller and add later if the business performs or the price becomes more attractive.
If your original thesis turns out to be wrong, you have committed less capital.
The smaller board lot does not remove risk.
It gives you more room to manage it.
One catch: trading costs still matter
Smaller lots do not mean investors should make tiny trades all the time.
If your broker charges a minimum commission, repeatedly buying $200 or $300 worth of shares can make transaction costs disproportionately high.
So the lesson is not:
Buy as little as possible.
It is:
Invest the amount that makes sense for your portfolio.
Get Smart: Start small, think about the whole portfolio
Looking back, I am slightly envious of someone starting to invest today.
Not because investing itself has become easier.
You still need to find good businesses, avoid overpaying, and sit through uncomfortable market declines.
But one unnecessary hurdle has become much smaller.
When I started investing, one lot of DBS could mean committing nearly S$14,000.
Today, investors have much more flexibility.
So instead of asking:
How much do I need to buy this stock?
Try asking:
How much of this stock do I actually want to own?
Because the real benefit of smaller board lots is not that we can buy more stocks.
It is that we can be more deliberate about how much of each stock we own.

title: Inflation-Proofing Your Kids: Why Cash Savings Might Be a Risk in 2026
article:
I remember it very clearly.
One of the first things I did when my daughter was born was to open a children’s savings account (and a Child Development Account, or CDA) for her.
The plan my husband and I had was to regularly put in a small amount every month, as well as
ang bao
money she would get from her first-month celebration or at future birthdays and even during the Chinese New Year season.
When our second and third children came along, we did the same for them.
The assumption was that this saving habit would build up to a nice, sizeable amount that they could eventually use for university tuition, their first home, or whatever big milestone lay ahead.
Seeing those account balances grow brought a great deal of comfort.
Unlike stock prices, cash feels solid and safe.
You deposit S$1,000, and six months later, it’s still S$1,000.
And maybe
that
is the problem.
Over time, while cash preserves the nominal digit in a bank book, it quietly destroys what that money can actually buy.
With university fees and daily living costs climbing across Singapore, holding too much cash for a long period presents a silent, ongoing challenge for our children’s future.
Why Cash Savings May Not Be as Safe as They Seem
Inflation acts like a silent tax on savings.
When prices rise, the purchasing power of every dollar shrinks.
To put this in perspective: at a steady 3% annual inflation rate, an expense costing S$10,000 today will shoot up to roughly S$18,061 in 20 years.
That means the S$10,000 you have in the bank today will not buy as much as it does now.
Singapore’s
core inflation
is projected to average 1.5% to 2.5% in 2026.
Meanwhile, basic kids’ savings accounts or standard bank deposits often yield base rates well below that mark.
Real return is what remains after subtracting inflation from your interest rate.
If your money earns a 1% base interest rate while inflation averages 3%, your real return is negative 2% each year – meaning your savings are steadily losing real-world value.
Unlike short-term adult savings, money set aside for a child often sits untouched for 10, 15, or even 20 years.
Over such long horizons, even tiny gaps between interest rates and inflation compound into massive losses in purchasing power.
The Real Cost of Raising and Educating a Child
As Prime Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted at the recent National Day Rally, the costs of raising and educating a child continue to weigh heavily on parents, prompting the government to step in with enhanced financial packages and reduced preschool fees.
For instance, under the newly announced
SG Child Support Package
, every Singaporean child will receive nearly S$70,000 in total direct financial support from birth to age 17 – including cash gifts, annual child credits, and post-secondary education top-ups.
While government support provides a welcome boost, the long-term price tag of major milestones remains significant.
University tuition and specialised enrichment programmes historically experience inflation rates that outpace general headline inflation.
Beyond tuition, many parents also hope to help their children with down payments for their first home or postgraduate studies.
Saving a fixed lump sum today without accounting for inflation leaves a shortfall decades down the road.
Rather than assume today’s costs will hold, map out when your child will need the funds and adjust expected expenses upward for inflation.

Of course, time helps cushion volatility, but it does not eliminate risk entirely.
Stock markets go through down cycles, and prices fluctuate.

How Parents Can Build Their Children’s Wealth Consistently
Building long-term wealth for your children does not require a massive lump sum upfront.
Here is how parents can build that foundation over time:

Putting even a modest
S$200 a month
into a low-cost ETF builds serious compounding momentum over 15 to 20 years.
Reinvest dividends and distributions:
Automatically reinvesting every payout buys more units along the way, quietly multiplying your portfolio’s long-term engine.
Review the portfolio as your child grows:
When your child nears major milestones around age 16 or 17, gradually shift those volatile growth holdings into safer, liquid cash assets to protect what you’ve built.
At the same time, we need to steer clear of a few common mistakes.
While leaving 100% of their money in cash guarantees a slow loss of buying power over time, jumping to the other extreme by chasing speculative, high-risk punts is equally dangerous.
Avoid investing without a clear horizon – putting money you’ll need in two years into equities leaves you exposed if the market takes a temporary dip.
Lastly, don’t miss the chance to
talk to your kids about money
along the way.
Teaching them how saving, interest, and compounding work in the real world ensures they inherit financial wisdom alongside the nest egg you’ve built for them.
Get Smart: Protect Their Future Purchasing Power
At the end of the day, cash isn’t the enemy.
It remains essential for emergency buffers, everyday expenses, and short-term peace of mind.
But holding a child’s entire long-term reserve in a standard bank account for 15 or 20 years quietly exposes their future to serious inflation risk.
The secret lies in matching every dollar to its timeline – keeping near-term funds in safe, liquid accounts while letting long-term money grow in a diversified investment portfolio.
By giving every dollar a clear job and a realistic time horizon, we can ensure the money we save for our children today actually retains its real buying power when they need it tomorrow.

title: Hong Kong IPO red flags include sudden loans and secret handshakes
article:
(Oct 14): Hong Kong’s markets watchdog has stepped up scrutiny of initial public offerings (IPOs) in one of the broadest enforcement actions in the city’s history, signalling a new level of concern about some practices in the booming market.

The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) on Tuesday suspended a stock and restricted dealing in HK$4.7 billion (US$599 million or $770 million) of assets across 31 brokerages as it took action against what it called IPO-rigging syndicates. It also warned banks further against arrangements that may artificially inflate demand for listings. In the same circular, the regulator listed what it sees as red flags when it comes to share sales.

“While most market participants play by the rules, intermediaries must remain alert to the warning signs associated with questionable arrangements, and challenge anything that does not add up,” SFC chief executive officer Julia Leung said in the statement. “The SFC will not hesitate to act against the few bad actors who seek to undermine a fair, orderly and quality market.”

Hong Kong is in the midst of a bumper year for IPO proceeds, driven by a series of listings by Chinese companies along the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain. As dealmaking ramped up, authorities have repeatedly warned of deal quality. Beijing has shared the concern and weighed tighter rules to increase the quality firms listing in Hong Kong, Bloomberg News reported earlier.

As the SFC warned market participants to be vigilant of “dubious arrangements”, here are the red flags the watchdog said can help identify potential issues:

Listing companies make substantial payments, loans or investments in favour of investors or connected parties, often very soon after the prospectus is finalised.

Sponsors should disclose any changes in the listing document since the last date of audited balance sheet to ensure the book is “complete and not misleading”, the SFC circular said.

See also: Segantii insider trading trial ends with verdict due February

Investors appear to be related to the company or executives, whose commitment to buy shares is “apparently made for business cooperation, investments or continued engagement”.

Syndicate banks should make inquiries with brokers on orders that “appear unusual or irregular”, or appear to be related to the issuer itself.

Bankers should be alarmed when the listing applicant is actively involved in investor selection, bookbuilding or allocation “beyond its ordinary role”, according to the circular. In some cases, the allocations may go against the agreed marketing, investor targeting or allocation strategy. The SFC particularly highlighted cases when the chosen investors had opened accounts with one or a few brokers just recently ahead of the listing.

The regulator also warned to be vigilant when companies receive unusual orders, including big tickets submitted shortly before closing the book — especially those that are disproportionate with the investors’ financial profile.

Bankers should inquire before helping these investors place orders, the regulator said.

One area of focus is arrangements to conceal ultimate investors, such as derivatives arrangements that provide exposure to the IPO shares with returns guaranteed by the issuer or the majority shareholder. In some cases, there are accounts of multiple investors controlled by the same entity.

While the price-to-list window shrank to two days from five since 2023, limiting time to check bids, the SFC on Tuesday urged bankers to take all reasonable steps to verify the identity of investors and only allocate shares to those who comply with requirements.

The regulator warned that in some cases, companies have pre-agreed commitments or other undisclosed arrangements with pre-IPO investors. In some cases, even if genuine demand is weak, the offer size and timetable may not be adjusted to reflect the market.

The SFC’s concerns extend to what happens to some stocks after the listing. Some arrangements may involve share concentration among designated investors, who have undisclosed arrangements concerning the company’s holdings or trading, including market capitalisation maintenance or turnover generation, it said. Corporate funds may be channelled by listing applicants to investors or connected parties before or after listing, the regulator added.

These activities pointed to inflated demand of IPO shares and may form part of a broader arrangement extending into manipulative post-listing trading activities. For sponsoring bankers, it could mean the prospectus contains false, misleading or incomplete disclosures.

With enforcement action under way and the SFC stepping up its warnings, the focus now turns to whether there will be penalties if anyone is found in breach.

In extreme cases, senior bankers can be held criminally liable, though the threshold to prove intent is high. For prospectus misstatements or material omissions, sponsors can be fined up to HK$700,000 or three years in prison. Those disseminating false or misleading information could be charged with market misconduct and fraudulent schemes, facing maximum penalties HK$10 million and a 10-year prison sentence.

Though Hong Kong has yet to dole out such harsh punishment, there have been cases of severe action. Bankers have been fined millions of dollars, reprimanded, banned from the market and banks have been suspended from IPO sponsoring work for various failures.

title: BHP cuts 300 workers at Australian iron ore mines as costs rise
article:
(Oct 14): BHP Group will make 300 workers redundant at its iron ore operations in Western Australia as it grapples with a fall in prices of the steelmaking ingredient and higher shipping and fuel costs.

Positions will be cut at its South Flank, Mining Area C, Newman and Jimblebar mines in the Pilbara region, which have a total workforce of around 16,000. The company will look at other employment opportunities for those affected, a BHP spokesperson said in a statement.

“We are making some changes to ensure our WA iron ore business can continue to make a significant contribution,” the spokesperson said.

Iron ore prices have fallen around 14% since the start of the year, while the costs of mining and shipping the raw material have increased in part due to surging fuel prices.

In its full-year financial report in August, BHP said the cost environment had “shifted materially” as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. “Higher energy prices have raised inflation across key regions, both directly and through their flow-on effects across supply chains,” it said.

BHP is not the only iron ore miner in the Pilbara to feel the impact of higher costs. Rio Tinto Group, its closest peer, said in its quarterly production report on Wednesday that elevated diesel prices have increased operating costs in the region by US$1 a tonne.

BHP expects to produce up to 298 million tonnes of iron ore in its current financial year, while Rio Tinto’s annual output sits at around 366 million tonnes.

title: Copper climbs to three-week high on strike threat, Fed comments
article:
(Oct 14): Copper rose toward US$14,700 a tonne as workers at the world’s biggest copper mine threatened imminent strike action while a Federal Reserve official played down the need for more than one additional rate hike this year.

Unions representing about a quarter of direct employees at BHP Group’s Escondida mine in Chile said a strike would begin from 8am local time on Wednesday after wage talks failed to produce an agreement. Any stoppage would add to a bumpy year for copper supply from Chile.

Copper reached a record near US$14,900 last month and has since hovered not far from that level against a backdrop of uncertainty about Fed policy and the impact of war in the Middle East. Data on US consumer prices due Wednesday will be closely watched as it could steer the Fed’s next move after September’s first hike since 2023.

Ahead of the inflation figures, the Fed’s Bank of New York President John Williams said he still sees one more interest-rate hike as appropriate this year and that he does not believe another will be necessary in 2027. Higher rates can be a headwind for metals by cooling the economy and raising costs.

Copper in London rose as much as 0.8% to US$14,695 a tonne — its highest since Sept 23 — before trading at US$14,666 by 12.29pm Shanghai time. Aluminium, nickel and zinc also advanced.

title: Singapore haze hits highest level as Indonesian fires worsen
article:
(Oct 14): A Singapore gauge of air quality worsened to the highest category in parts of the city-state on Wednesday, as swathes of Southeast Asia choked on haze from wildfires raging in Indonesia.

The one-hour reading of the average concentration of fine particulate matter reached 288 in the west of Singapore, National Environment Agency data show. Levels of 251 and above are considered “very high”, the top of its four-category system. Readings in the city-state’s four other regions were in the “elevated” and “high” categories as of Wednesday afternoon.

Much of the smog stems from smoke drifting from neighbouring Indonesia, which is suffering through its worst wildfire season in years. Prolonged dryness, exacerbated by a powerful El Niño, has created conditions for land-clearing fires to burn out of control and emit noxious fumes, fuelling health and diplomatic concerns across the region.

Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and the Indonesian city of Medan in Sumatra were the three most-polluted cities in the world as of Wednesday afternoon, according to data compiled by IQAir.

Pollution has also been high in parts of Malaysia, with schools in cities including Johor and Melaka closed on Wednesday. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim contacted Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto last week about efforts to tackle the smog, and the country’s foreign minister said Malaysia will seek more effective regional mechanisms to address transboundary haze.

Singapore’s Ministry of Education judges school closures based on another air-quality measure, the 24-hour Pollution Standards Index. If the PSI forecast for the next day is in the highest category — “hazardous” — school closures will be considered.

See also: Wildfire haze shuts Malaysian schools and looms over Singapore F1

PSI readings in all five regions were in the “unhealthy” range as of early afternoon, the third level in the government’s five-step scale. Some sports facilities in the west of the city-state were closed on Wednesday.

Aerial firefighting efforts in Indonesia have recently been hampered by poor visibility. However, the country is repurposing a weather-modification technique pioneered in the 1940s in its latest effort to fight the pollution. Aircraft will disperse pellets of dry ice above South Sumatra province in an experimental approach that authorities hope will reduce the hazardous smoke.

The number of hotspots in Indonesia have reached 7,530 this month, the most in October since 2015, according to the Indonesian Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi. A hotspot is defined as a location where satellites detect an elevated surface temperature, indicating a potential fire.

See also: Singapore, Malaysia cloaked in haze before key sports events

Dry conditions are expected to persist over much of southern Southeast Asia in the coming days, aside from Peninsular Malaysia and northern and central parts of Sumatra and Borneo, according to the NEA’s website.

Indonesia has forecast its rainy season will be shorter and later than usual this year, starting in November or December.

title: Canada aims for India trade deal by year-end, minister says
article:
(Oct 14): Canada will seek to conclude a trade deal with India by the end of the year as the two countries look to strengthen economic ties and diversify partnerships amid growing global uncertainty.

Negotiators from India and Canada began a fifth round of talks from Oct 5, building on discussions that concluded last month. India Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December and sign a completed trade deal.

“The momentum is there, the energy is there to get it done,” Maninder Sidhu, Canadian International Trade Minister, said in an interview with Haslinda Amin. “Hopefully we will get it done this year. That is the focus.”

The push to deepen economic ties with India comes as Canada faces rising trade tensions with the US following the breakdown of negotiations between the two countries. India, meanwhile, is contending with fresh tariff threats from a new law that gives US President Donald Trump the power to impose levies of as much as 100% on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

Canada sees opportunities to deepen ties with India in mining and food security while also identifying infrastructure investment and nuclear energy as areas for deeper cooperation.

He signalled Ottawa’s interest in participating in India’s expansion plans.

See also: Vietnam says US trade deal nearly done with final text sent

“As India grows, Canada grows. We want to support India,” Sidhu said. “We can help India build all the supply chains. Negotiations are always tough but we are going to do what is best for our businesses.”

Nuclear energy is another potential area of cooperation. India is opening up its tightly controlled nuclear industry to private companies as it seeks to rapidly expand atomic power generation. That could create opportunities for Canada, which has some of the world’s largest uranium resources as well as nuclear technology and expertise, to supply fuel and participate in new projects.

title: Imminent retrenchment in AI investment not expected: MAS
article:
Singapore’s economic expansion will continue into 2027 on the back of the global AI investment cycle, says the Monetary Authority (MAS) in their latest, quarterly macroeconomic review on Oct 14. The central bank does not expect an immediate retrenchment in AI investments even though it notes that hyperscalers have been facing some pressure on their financial buffers.

While MAS expects Singapore’s technology-led expansion to continue in the coming quarters, it adds that the city-state’s economy should grow at a more measured pace next year.

To track the development of the global AI investment cycle, MAS’s Economic Policy Group constructed two indices: the Global Semiconductor Production Index (GSPI) and the Hyperscaler Capex Cover Index (HCCI).

The GSPI tracks cyclical conditions in the semiconductor sector while the HCCI monitors changes in the hyperscalers’ capacity to sustain capex spending based on their cash-flow generation, leverage and investment intensity. MAS says the indices show that strong semiconductor production growth has held up despite the strains on the finances of the hyperscalers.

“Even if rising financial vulnerabilities raise the risks of a pullback in AI capex, substantial order backlogs and committed capacity buildouts should cushion the near-term impact on production,” MAS adds.

“Together with the strengthening domestic electronics PMI (Purchasing Managers' Index) and increases in new orders and order backlogs, these indicators suggest that the AI-led semiconductor cycle is more likely to remain in a phase of expansion.”

MAS said in its annual Financial Stability Review (FSR) on Sept 22 that a retrenchment in AI-related investments could have a serious impact on the global economy. The combination of growing fiscal pressures and surging energy costs, coupled with AI’s capital-intensive nature, have resulted in a higher cost of capital and hurdle rate for AI investment.

“A material shortfall in earnings or expected returns could trigger a broader reassessment of AI-related valuations, with losses propagating across public equity, corporate bond and private credit markets,” MAS said in its FSR.

Earlier this month, on Oct 8, OpenAI reported that its annualised revenue at the end of September was about US$50 billion ($64 billion), much lower than an earlier estimate of US$70 billion it gave in September. The revenue miss spooked AI investors and sparked a sell-off in tech companies like Nvidia and Microsoft.

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan has brushed aside investor concerns over OpenAI’s revenue numbers. Tan, who was speaking at DBS’s inaugural Asia Future Forward Conference on Oct 12, says OpenAI’s annualised revenue of US$50 billion is a decent performance for a startup.

“It means nothing at all. All it means is a lot of investors investing in AI have no clue what they are investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino, gambling,” Tan says.

Higher energy costs due to the war in Iran are expected to persist in the immediate months ahead, MAS says in its report. The central bank expects both oil and non-oil imported inflation to remain elevated only in the near term before it begins to ease more discernibly from mid-2027 onwards. This is because gradually normalising supply conditions and modest domestic cost pressures will help to temper inflation.

MAS core inflation is projected to come in at around 1.5% to 2.0% in 2026 and 1.5% to 2.5% in 2027. Headline inflation, or CPI-All Item Inflation, is forecasted to be at around 2.0% in 2026 and between 1.5% to 2.5% in 2027.

“For now, the risks to inflation remain tilted towards the upside. Further adverse geopolitical shocks could lead to another sharp increase in global energy prices, and more prolonged shortages of key refined products and intermediate goods,” MAS says in its macroeconomic review.

MAS said in a separate statement on Oct 14 that it was keeping its monetary policy unchanged. It had previously tightened the rate of appreciation of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) consecutively in both April and July. Singapore relies on the exchange rate instead of interest rates to manage its monetary policy.

“The current appreciating policy band will allow the S$NEER to continue to strengthen and lean against the anticipated near-term rise in imported inflation, ensuring the gradual easing of inflationary pressures in 2027,” MAS said in its quarterly policy statement.

title: IMF, World Bank tout Bangkok blueprint against digital fraud
article:
(Oct 14): The International Monetary Fund and World Bank unveiled a global roadmap to fight online financial fraud as increasingly sophisticated scams undermine confidence in digital finance.

The “Bangkok Blueprint” — developed in coordination with the Bank of Thailand and released during the institutions’ annual meetings on Wednesday in Bangkok — sets out 12 policy considerations to help countries identify vulnerabilities and develop comprehensive and coordinated responses, Thai central bank chief Vitai Ratanakorn said.

“The framework calls for a whole-of-ecosystem response, stronger cross-border cooperation, and sharing practical experience to inform evolving global standard setting,” Vitai said during the report launch, adding that it drew experiences from Hong Kong, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. Asia accounted for 67% of global fraud losses in 2024, he said.

Scam operations have been proliferating across Southeast Asia in recent years, particularly in border regions adjacent to Thailand, which has become a transit hub for human trafficking linked to scam compounds.

The initiative comes as Thailand’s efforts to crack down on scam operations have uncovered sophisticated ways in which proceeds of cyber fraud become a major part of the broader illicit financial flow, Vitai said. Fraud losses exceeded 43 billion baht in 2024, before falling to 32 billion baht in 2025. “Coordinated action can make a meaningful difference,” said Vitai, under whose leadership the central bank has taken a more active role in tracing and blocking illicit money flows.

Globally, cyber events in the financial sector have increased tenfold over the past decade, while cyber-enabled fraud cases have roughly tripled, according to an infographic accompanying the blueprint. The figures likely understate the scale of the problem because of significant underreporting and often rudimentary reporting systems. Some 90% of the 165 jurisdictions assessed by the Bangkok Blueprint consider fraud a major money-laundering threat.

See also: Singapore updates national cybersecurity strategy to protect essential services

“When we started discussing the blueprint, we did believe it was important,” IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said during the session. “And then we came to Bangkok, with AI putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids, and that is now even more important.”

The framework spans legal foundations, fraud prevention and enforcement, domestic and international cooperation and consumer protection. It emphasises clear accountability and timely coordination across financial services, social media, digital platforms, e-commerce and telecommunications networks.

The institutions said that while digital finance has widened access and improved efficiency, it’s also enabled fraud to spread faster and become more sophisticated.

See also: Agentic AI is changing the economics of cybercrime

“Fraud has no borders,” Thailand Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said. “So our response should be cross borders as well.”

title: Vietnam says US trade deal nearly done with final text sent
article:
(Oct 14): Vietnam has “essentially completed” talks on a US trade deal and submitted its final remarks to Washington after months of negotiations over tariffs and other trade barriers.

“We have sent the final comments to the US side and if both sides agree on this, we will sign the deal soon,” Vietnam Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc said at a US-Vietnam business summit in Hanoi on Wednesday. “It will open up greater opportunities for businesses in both countries.”

An agreement would give exporters greater certainty as Vietnam faces the threat of additional US tariffs from ongoing trade investigations. The Southeast Asian manufacturing hub has spent months negotiating with Washington, with transshipment and non-tariff barriers among the main sticking points.

“[US] President Trump is clear that trade must be balanced and reciprocal,” Jennifer Wicks, US Ambassador to Vietnam, said at the event, noting that the two governments continue to negotiate an agreement. American firms seeking to invest in Vietnam need the right conditions to do so with confidence, she said, adding that investment depends on clear and predictable laws and regulations.

The two countries are “very close” to a trade deal, Vietnam President To Lam told Bloomberg News in an interview last month. Vietnam has repeatedly pledged to buy more US high-tech goods, including aircraft and liquefied natural gas, as it seeks to narrow its trade surplus with its largest export market.

Factories continue to send record shipments to the US despite the risk of further tariffs. Exports helped drive economic growth to 9.95% in the third quarter, putting the government’s double-digit target for the year within reach.

See also: IMF says US growth not enough to fight high debt, deficit levels

The trade surplus with the US widened 23.8% to US$122.6 billion in the first nine months from a year earlier, according to Vietnamese data. The country ranks alongside Mexico, Taiwan and China among economies running the largest trade imbalances with the US.

“Hanoi now needs to make bold moves to address this trade imbalance,” Michael George DeSombre, US Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, said in video remarks at the event. Concluding the deal would help rebalance trade, he said, highlighting the need to address non-tariff barriers including motor vehicle safety and emissions standards, among others.

“In this regard, I strongly encourage Vietnam to look carefully at those industries where foreign ownership is capped, particularly those where it is capped below 50%,” DeSombre added.

See also: World economy holds up but nears limits of resilience, IMF says

In addition to the 12.5% tariff applied to most Vietnamese goods entering the US, findings from American trade probes into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and intellectual property violations could result in higher levies on the country’s manufacturers. That has added pressure on negotiators to finalise an agreement.

As Vietnam pursues 10% growth, pressure is growing on an electricity market that the government is seeking to overhaul. Vietnam Prime Minister Le Minh Hung has called for a review of power projects that are behind schedule, as plans to rapidly expand LNG imports run into red tape and financial hurdles that have delayed nearly all of the country’s proposed developments.

Energy project developers need policies that are “consistent and facilitate investment", Wicks said. They also need clear rules on pricing, dispatch and direct power purchases, she added. “Getting these terms right will determine whether Vietnam’s power plans generate power plants.”

title: ASML boosts outlook as demand for chip tools outpaces supply
article:
(Oct 14): ASML Holding NV boosted its 2026 sales forecast and said soaring artificial intelligence spending meant that it will not be able to fully meet demand for its chip-making machines in the next two years.

The Veldhoven, Netherlands-based firm projected annual sales of between €44 billion and €45 billion this year, it said in a statement Wednesday. The low end of the range was previously €43 billion.

ASML said its current supply plans mean it will not be able to fully meet demand in 2027 and 2028. “We are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase we previously communicated,” CEO Christophe Fouquet said in the statement.

ASML’s results can provide a window into chipmakers’ plans because the company’s advanced tools have a lead time of more than a year between order and delivery. Industry players are increasingly questioning whether the AI boom is sustainable. There was a global selloff in semiconductor stocks this week after Broadcom Inc CEO Hock Tan likened investor sentiment in the industry to a casino.

Investors have flagged concerns about whether ASML can fulfil orders while the market is hot. In July, ASML said it plans to boost capacity by 30% next year for its second-most advanced tool, the low-NA extreme ultraviolet lithography machine, which would take its annual shipment target to about 85 units.

See also: Musk says Terrafab plant to ‘make chips better than anyone’

The chip-gear-maker's customers have boosted their equipment demand forecasts based on the “size and duration of AI-related investments", Fouquet said. Some customers “are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030”, he said.

ASML is the only company that makes the cutting-edge lithography machines used to produce semiconductors for the data centres powering the AI boom. Its outlook offers an indication of investment plans by chipmakers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, Samsung Electronics Co and Intel Corp as spending on AI infrastructure surges.

The company is working to ship tools faster to customers by reducing the cycle time or the period between starting production in its clean rooms and shipping a completed machine. It began construction on its second industrial campus in the Netherlands, the first phase of which is set to be completed in 2029.

See also: Nvidia soars near US$6 tril market cap with stock back at high

The AI spending spree propelled ASML to become Europe’s most valuable company, with its shares up 64% so far this year.

Net sales in the July to September quarter rose to €11.66 billion, ASML said. That compares with the average analyst estimate of €11.7 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The company sold 17 EUV machines in the quarter while revenue from the service and upgrades of machines already installed at customers’ sites increased 19% in the quarter as chipmakers looked to be more productive.

“Against the backdrop of an overall 36% increase in 2026 in comparison to 2025, you see that that is largely driven by EUV,” chief financial officer Roger Dassen said in a video accompanying the results. “So the EUV business grows over 45% this year.”

South Korea remained ASML’s largest market for new system tools in the third quarter, followed by Taiwan and China. China is expected to account for about 20% of ASML’s total revenue this year.

Last quarter, top chipmakers announced plans to order ASML’s most sophisticated chipmaking tool, which costs US$400 million per unit. Samsung and TSMC said they would begin to mass produce chips with high NA EUV tools by 2028 and 2030, respectively. Intel Corp said in September it had already processed more than a million wafers using the technology.

There are also growing concerns over the potential dangers of AI. Companies including OpenAI and Anthropic PBC have revealed a number of incidents in which models behaved in unsanctioned ways. These disclosures have fuelled concerns about AI security risks, prompting talk about slowing or pausing development of cutting-edge AI.

Microsoft Corp CEO Satya Nadella recently called for exercising restraint, adding that those deploying advanced AI shouldn’t only depend on assurances from AI model makers.

title: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows
article:
(Oct 14): Oil climbed as a flare-up in attacks in the Middle East increased uncertainty over a recovery in Persian Gulf energy flows.

Brent rose above US$106 a barrel after falling 0.9% on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) advanced towards US$95. An escalation of Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz is threatening the rebound in Gulf supply to near prewar levels, although the US said it assisted in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude through the waterway.

Elsewhere in the region, Saudi Arabia intercepted more missiles and drones launched by Yemen’s Houthis, as fighting with the Iran-backed militant group showed few signs of subsiding. The headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco in the east of the kingdom was hit in the latest attacks.

Brent has surged more than 70% this year as the US-Iran war roils energy markets. Risks intensified after the Houthis attacked Riyadh’s main airport last week and Saudi-backed forces launched a campaign to reclaim rebel-held territory in Yemen. Ship strikes in Hormuz have also prompted more supertankers to turn away from the Persian Gulf.

“Crude oil exports continue, but uncertainty around it remains elevated,” Morgan Stanley analysts including Martijn Rats said in a note, in which the bank raised its forecast for physical benchmark Dated Brent by US$5 a barrel for this quarter and the next. “At the same time, attacks on Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure have increased.”

The renewed strikes on the kingdom are adding pressure on Washington to step up support for its ally. US President Donald Trump said he might ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to join the response to the Houthis’ attacks on the kingdom.

See also: Trump’s diesel deal irks allies and is unlikely to reduce prices

Still, Saudi oil output has continued to recover. The kingdom reported to Opec that its crude production jumped by a third last month, recovering from the lowest in more than three decades, but remaining well below prewar levels.

In Europe, Trump defended his diesel export agreement with Russia, saying the supply would be released onto the global market to ease high prices and was “not for us”. Republican senators earlier urged him to scrap the deal, which would upend years of sanctions, calling it “a gift to our adversary” and a betrayal of US allies, according to a copy of the letter posted on X by an Axios reporter.

See also: Trump lifts sanctions, says Russia to supply diesel to US, world
• Brent for December settlement advanced 0.6% to US$106.32 a barrel at 6.17am in London.

title: Gold steady as Fed official’s remarks temper rate-hike bets
article:
(Oct 14): Gold held a two-day decline after a Federal Reserve official signalled one more interest-rate hike may be needed this year but further tightening will not be necessary in 2027, improving sentiment toward the precious metal.

Bullion traded near US$4,170 an ounce, after falling 0.8% in the previous two sessions. Oil rose as a flare-up in attacks in the Middle East threatened further energy disruptions that could weigh on inflation and make a case for higher borrowing costs. Brent crude was above US$106 a barrel.

Fed New York President John Williams said he sees one more interest-rate hike as appropriate this year. US Treasury yields edged lower after his remarks, supporting gold, which typically does better in a lower-rate environment as it does not pay interest.

US consumer price index data due later on Wednesday may provide clues on the Fed’s rate path, after it hiked for the first time since 2023 last month. Swaps traders are pricing in a low chance of a rise at this month’s policy meeting but see roughly 90% odds of an increase in December.

Gold’s price action of late has been muted despite large-scale selling by trend-following funds, Daniel Ghali, head of metals research at Deutsche Bank AG wrote in a note. There’s “robust physical demand for gold, with non-commercial and commercial flows working together to offset algo sales and retail now on the sidelines,” he said.

See also: Gold steadies as traders assess US-Iran tensions, Fed rate path

Spot gold rose 0.1% to US$4,163.82 an ounce as of 11.35am Singapore time while silver was 0.1% higher at US$59.20. Platinum was flat while palladium advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was 0.1% lower.

title: IMF says US growth not enough to fight high debt, deficit levels
article:
(Oct 14): The head of the IMF said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s plan to grow the economy out of its mounting debt and fiscal deficit problems won’t work fast enough.

“The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the US,” Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday. “Growth, of course, helps but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments.”

“Some measures would be necessary,” she added, speaking in Bangkok during the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings.

Bessent, who isn’t attending this week’s gathering, has said in recent months that the US will be able to change its debt and deficit trajectory through a reliance on strong economic growth.

“What is important is the debt-to-GDP, and we will start bending that curve and bringing it down,” Bessent said last week. “It could happen very quickly.”

He added that consistent gross domestic product growth above 3%, a target set to be hit for the last quarter of the year, will help secure the goal.

See also: World economy holds up but nears limits of resilience, IMF says

Meanwhile, US debt is heading into unprecedented territory, one of the key reasons behind a surge in long-term borrowing costs that has raised alarm bells globally.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) in February warned the debt-to-GDP ratio in 2030 will exceed a record 106% set in 1946. Total US public debt has surpassed US$40 trillion ($51 trillion) for the first time, with a surge of a third in less than five years.

And the deficit has reached US$2 trillion and is on track to pass 6% of gross domestic product this fiscal year, the CBO said.

See also: HSBC moves to Wall Street bonus model, cuts fixed-pay deals

CBO director Phillip Swagel projected last week that the US would need to grow at least 5% annually to stabilise the federal debt levels, assuming an interest-rate level of 4%. At a higher interest rate of 5% — roughly the current level — the US would need 6% GDP growth, adjusting for inflation.

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg see the US on track for a growth rate of a little over 2%, adjusted for inflation, for this year.

Alongside growth, Bessent has also vowed to put forward a fiscal consolidation package to reduce spending, saying since August that he’s working with Office of Management and Budget director Russ Vought on the plan. However, hasn’t offered any public details.

The Treasury Department didn’t respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

Bessent skipped the IMF meetings this week, as well as a gathering of Group of 20 finance ministers he was expected to lead. The US is also the most important member of the IMF, as it has the biggest voting share.

The US delegation this week is being led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke and Erin Browne, the undersecretary for international affairs. Bessent skipped a similar G20 meeting in South Africa last year as well.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

On the broader issue of global imbalances, Georgieva said Wednesday that the IMF has been “ringing the alarm bell on excessive global imbalances growing”.

“We need to look at who are the biggest contributors, and they are primarily China and US,” she said, adding that China needs to boost domestic consumption while other economies must focus on lowering debt and deficit levels and spend less.

The gap between surplus savers like China and Japan and deficit economies like the US is back at the highest level since the lead-up to the 2007-08 global financial crisis, and is nearing a 150-year peak, a level that has preceded past turmoil.

“To put it very simply,” she said. “China needs to spend more. The US has to save more, and Europe has to invest more.”

title: China’s trade surplus nears US$1 tril again with export surge
article:
(Oct 14): China’s trade surplus ballooned to US$938 billion for the first nine months, keeping it on pace to exceed last year’s record as export growth surged faster than expected in September.

Exports soared 36% last month from a year earlier — the fastest since February — after an increase of 25% in August. Imports jumped 31%, data released by China’s General Administration of Customs showed on Wednesday.

As a result, the trade surplus for September widened to US$133.5 billion, compared with the median estimate of US$117.8 billion in a Bloomberg survey of economists. Its year-to-date level is on track to hit US$1 trillion or more already this month — crossing a threshold that wasn’t reached until November in 2025.

China’s lopsided trade relations with the world have grown even more extreme since the tariff war started by US President Donald Trump over a year ago, especially as global demand exploded for AI services and inputs like chips.

Facing higher barriers in the US, Chinese companies have sought out new markets abroad, with the International Monetary Fund estimating that emerging and advanced Asian economies absorbed about half of the diverted trade, followed by the European Union with near one-fifth.

See also: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China

But as domestic demand stagnates, the booming exports are also generating more pushback from China’s largest trade partners. After months of standoff with the EU, Brussels and Beijing have agreed to cap imports of hybrid cars from China, according to the bloc, though China describes the deal as ensuring “export space and steady growth” for its carmakers.

China reported a record trade surplus of US$34.8 billion with the EU in September, before the two sides announced results from months of negotiations. It was almost 21% higher than in the same month a year ago.

The number of countries running trade deficits above 3% of their gross domestic product with China more than tripled since 2005 to 82 last year, according to economists at Goldman Sachs Group Inc, who estimate that most of them are low-income emerging economies.

title: Princeton Digital Group seeks US$1.2 bil loan for Malaysia data centre — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 14): Asian data centre operator Princeton Digital Group Ltd is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion ($1.5 billion) to fund its Malaysia buildout, according to a person familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure continues.

HSBC Holdings plc Singapore branch, Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore) Ltd, and United Overseas Bank Ltd are the mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for the three-year loan deal, said the person, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

Proceeds from the loan to be taken by the company’s subsidiary, Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha Ltd, will be used to fund a 198.8-megawatt data centre campus project in Johor, Malaysia, and to refinance existing debt, the person said.

Standard Chartered declined to comment. Representatives for Princeton Digital Group, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Data centre companies across the world have been taking on debt as they seek to raise capital to meet growing AI demand. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt.

But there are signs global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations as evidenced by the collapse of Nvidia Corp-backed data centre operator Firmus Grid Ltd’s initial public offering last week.

See also: DayOne inks RM15 bil multi-currency financing arrangement with seven banks

Data centre firm AirTrunk, which counts Blackstone Inc as a key investor, was reported to delay its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until next year as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand.

Headquartered in Singapore, Princeton Digital’s top shareholder is Warburg Pincus and other investors include Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment Co and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board.

The firm, founded in 2018, operates more than 1.8 gigawatts of data centre capacity across Asia including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, according to its website.

See also: Data centre outages may leave Apac operators with uninsured losses, says Howden

PDG has been on a borrowing spree as it seeks to expand across Asia. In May, the firm said it raised around US$856 million for its data centre buildout in Indonesia. Earlier in the year, the company said it was targeting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support regional expansion plans.

title: Hongkong Land to seek stake in tycoon Ong Beng Seng’s Singapore assets — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 14): Hongkong Land Holdings Ltd is in discussions with Ong Beng Seng’s Hotel Properties Ltd to buy a majority stake in three buildings in Singapore’s Orchard Road shopping belt, according to people familiar with the matter.

A potential deal could involve the developer, controlled by Hong Kong’s Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd, investing in the three adjacent properties earmarked for development, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters. The assets comprise hotel voco Orchard, shopping mall Forum, and HPL House, which houses Hotel Properties’ headquarters and Hard Rock Cafe.

Discussions are still at an early stage and could conclude without a deal, the people said. A stake sale will likely value the assets at over $2 billion, although that is subject to change, they said.

A Hongkong Land spokesperson declined to comment. Christopher Lim, Hotel Properties’ group executive director, declined to comment when contacted by phone.

A successful transaction will mark a respite for Hotel Properties, which has faced challenges after its co-founder Ong was convicted last year in a scandal that led to the imprisonment of a senior politician in Singapore. The Malaysian tycoon, who controls the firm with his wife Christina through a roughly 60% stake, relinquished his decades-long tenure as managing director of the company, citing medical conditions. He avoided a jail sentence and was fined.

Hotel Properties has been looking to reduce its stakes in the voco hotel and Forum mall, excluding HPL House, people familiar with the matter said last year. The firm is now including HPL House in the assets put up for sale after talks with other interested parties fell through, the people said.

See also: Singapore property investment sales hit $42.2 bil in 9M2026, surpassing 2025: Knight Frank

Hotel Properties was given provisional government approval in 2023 to redevelop the three properties into a mixed project comprising a hotel, retail, office and residential components, as well as a rooftop garden and a performance theatre.

As the sale of assets got underway, the redevelopment plans made some potential partners baulk due to uncertainties, the people said. These include concerns over the theatre’s profitability, and the lack of income for years arising from a big transformation, which is already likely to require significant capital outlay, they said.

Hotel Properties’ Lim said at a shareholders’ meeting in April that the company was evaluating the redevelopment carefully as it would involve giving up recurring income from the properties. It was “focused on optimising development potential with the relevant authorities, including seeking revisions to certain approved parameters”.

See also: Hong Kong lifeline buys Cheng family time to save New World

The company swung to a net loss of $39.1 million in the first half of 2026, compared with a profit of $11.4 million a year earlier. Its shares have fallen 6% over the past one year, compared with a 25% gain in the benchmark Straits Times Index.

For Hongkong Land, a purchase of the assets will expand its presence in Singapore’s retail strip. A new fund backed by the firm said in July it was buying Wheelock Place mall for $1.1 billion from long-time owner Wharf Real Estate Investment Co. Wharf’s controlling shareholder Hong Kong billionaire Peter Woo also owns about a fifth of Hotel Properties’ shares.

title: Hyundai Motor to invest US$15.5 bil in India through 2032
article:
(Oct 14): Hyundai Motor Group plans to invest US$15.5 billion in India through 2032, positioning the South Asian nation as a core piece of its future growth strategy.

The investment spans manufacturing expansion for both the Hyundai and Kia brands, research and development, infrastructure, its local supply chain and technology, the company said in a stock exchange filing late Tuesday. Hyundai said it aims to make India one of its leading vehicle export hubs globally.

Shares of Hyundai Motor India Ltd jumped as much as 2.5% on Wednesday in Mumbai, putting shares on track for a fourth day of gains. The benchmark NSE Nifty 50 Index had inched up as much as 0.2%.

India has become a core market for the South Korean automaker, last year accounting for about 15% of its global sales volume and becoming its third-largest region. By 2030, the Hyundai group has said it aims to make India its second-largest region behind only North America.

“This investment reaffirms our commitment to India for the next 30 years and beyond,” executive chair Chung Euisun said in a statement following a meeting between him and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi.

Hyundai currently has the capacity to produce more than 1.4 million vehicles a year in India across three plants — Hyundai Motor Co factories in Chennai and Pune, as well as Kia Corp’s Anantapur facility. The group said the new funding will support “significant volume growth" but did not provide specifics on how and where it will be spent.

See also: Jio Platforms said to draw more than US$20 bil in bids for IPO in India

Hyundai previously announced plans to invest US$5.1 billion in India through 2030.

India is one of the few major markets worldwide expected to see continued growth in auto sales at a time when global demand is stalling. Legacy automakers like Hyundai that have localised production skirt high tariffs and import quotas that have blunted Chinese and other automaker brands’ advance into the subcontinent.

José Muñoz, Hyundai’s CEO, sees India as a promising opportunity at a time when his company faces industry challenges in other key markets such as US tariffs, excess capacity in China and stepped up competition in Europe.

“Nowadays, we have the Middle East in war, in America we have a lot of issues going on, in Europe we have the Chinese competition. So how do we handle them?” he said Tuesday at a Bloomberg New Economy Forum event in New Delhi.

Noting Hyundai’s plan to launch some 26 new vehicles in the country by 2030, Muñoz said, “Now India is the star.”

title: Parkway Life REIT to acquire another three nursing homes in France for €38.8 mil
article:
Parkway Life REIT is acquiring three nursing homes in France from the regular partner DomusVi Group for €38.8 million, or some $56.5 million.

The homes, which will come with a 12-year lease, are located in and around Marseille, France’s second-largest city, and will continue to be operated by DomusVi, described as the third largest aged care operator in France, running some 600 homes and facilities.

Upon completion, the REIT will own 14 properties in France, valued at $234.3 million.

PLifeREIT says the lease structure also provides a natural hedge against inflationary pressures, supporting the sustainability of rental income amid rising operating costs and interest rate volatility.

In total, the REIT expects to spend €43.4 million, which consists of the total acquisition outlay, including estimated capitalised and acquisition-related costs.

The acquisition, to be debt funded, will raise the REIT's aggregate leverage from 33.8% as at June 30 to 35.3%.

See also: Starhill Global REIT divests Ebisu Fort for JPY6.2 bil, 53.8% above valuation

"This acquisition represents another measured step in scaling PLife REIT’s presence in France, our third key market," says Yong Yean Chau, the REIT manager's CEO and executive director.

"Building on our partnership with DomusVi since 2024, this offmarket transaction expands our footprint in France and positions us to capture further growth opportunities.

"The long-term leases also provide greater income visibility and resilience, supporting sustainable returns to our unitholders," he adds.

title: Asian stocks rise on signal Fed may not need aggressive rate hikes
article:
(Oct 14): Asian stocks bounced on Wednesday after two days of losses on expectations the US Federal Reserve (Fed) may not need to raise interest rates aggressively next year. American crude extended its rally.

MSCI Inc’s Asia-Pacific equities index advanced 0.2%. A sell-off in semiconductor stocks sent the gauge to its weakest close since August on Tuesday.

Earlier, the S&P 500 pared earlier losses to close little changed after New York Fed president John Williams said he continued to see one more rate hike as appropriate this year but no need for further tightening in 2027. Pressure on tech stocks eased and Microsoft Corp rose to a record.

Treasuries rallied and the dollar fell in the New York session, with traders looking to Wednesday’s US consumer price inflation data for further clues on the path of interest rates.

US oil rose 0.8% to about US$94.80 ($121.38) a barrel, extending its advance to a fifth session, as a flare-up in Middle East attacks increased uncertainty over a recovery in energy shipments from the Persian Gulf. Global benchmark Brent climbed 0.7% to US$106.40 a barrel.

See also: ICE plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group

Williams’ comments offered some relief ahead of the key inflation data, with markets concerned that elevated oil prices could keep price pressures persistent. Traders are also looking to earnings for clues on the direction of the artificial intelligence trade, which has come under pressure amid doubts that billions of dollars in spending will deliver commensurate returns.

“The prospect of fewer Fed hikes should give Asian stocks some breathing room today,” said Josh Gilbert, the lead Asia-Pacific analyst at eToro. “Williams talking down an extended tightening cycle has taken some heat out of yields, and that’s welcome news for tech stocks across Asia.”
